title: The loops: cerebellum, basal ganglia and gait
description: How the cerebellum and basal ganglia shape movement without powering it, how to localize ataxia, vertigo and involuntary movements, and why watching a child walk is the best single test of the motor system.
why: The cerebellum and basal ganglia shape movement without weakening it, and their disorders show most clearly when a child walks.
objectives: Explain why cerebellar and basal ganglia disease spare strength, and check strength before calling a movement ataxic.
Localize cerebellar signs by side and by midline versus hemisphere.
Work through acute ataxia in a child in order of danger and likelihood.
Describe involuntary movements precisely, and read a gait as a tour of the levels of the neuraxis.

sections.title: Two circuits that move nothing directly
sections.content:
Two of the brain's great motor circuits move nothing on their own, because neither the cerebellum nor the basal ganglia sends its own fibers to the anterior horn cells. Both work in loops, taking in what the cortex intends and what the body reports and sending their verdict back, through the thalamus, to the motor cortex that will act on it. Pearl calls the cerebellum "the great modulator of the nervous system" (Pearl 2014, p. 116), and the phrase fits the basal ganglia too. The cerebellar loop tunes the accuracy and timing of movement, while the basal ganglia loop sets how much movement is allowed and how fast it runs.

**Why this changes the exam**

Because these loops shape movement rather than power it, their disease leaves **strength intact**. A child with cerebellar disease is clumsy, overshoots and walks on a broad base, yet pushes against your hand normally, and a child with basal ganglia disease has too little movement or too much of the wrong kind, with no paralysis. The practical consequence is that you should prove a limb is strong before you call its movement ataxic or dystonic, because a weak arm also misses the target and a weak child also falls. That is why the [[m03-first-fork|first fork]] comes before any question about coordination.

**Two kinds of wrong movement**

- **Cerebellar** disorders produce errors in range, rate and rhythm, seen as dysmetria on finger-nose testing, irregular rapid alternating movements, an intention tremor that grows as the hand approaches the target, a wide-based gait, nystagmus and scanning speech (Pearl 2014, pp. 63, 116).
- **Basal ganglia** disorders produce errors in amount and selection, with slowness and rigidity at one end and chorea, dystonia, tics and other unwanted movements at the other.

Tremor offers a practical way to tell the two apart, since a cerebellar tremor appears on action and worsens near the target, whereas a tremor at rest belongs to the basal ganglia.

**In a child**

Clumsiness is one of the commonest reasons a child is referred, and most clumsy children have neither a cerebellar nor a basal ganglia lesion. The developmental exam therefore asks first whether the clumsiness is simply appropriate for the child's age. The toddler's broad-based, jerky, falling gait is normal at the age when walking begins (DeMyer, p. 338), and localization starts only when a sign is abnormal for the child in front of you.
keyPoints: The cerebellum and basal ganglia work in loops back to the motor cortex, shaping movement without powering it.
Because their disease spares strength, a limb must be shown to be strong before its movement is called ataxic or dystonic.
Cerebellar errors are errors of range, rate and rhythm, and basal ganglia errors are errors of amount and selection.
An action tremor that worsens near the target is cerebellar, and a tremor at rest comes from the basal ganglia.

question.question: A 7-year-old overshoots badly on finger-nose testing with the right arm. Strength in that arm is 3 out of 5, with brisk right reflexes. What is the most defensible description?
options: Right cerebellar ataxia, calling for imaging of the posterior fossa
Right arm weakness of upper motor neuron type, which means the overshoot cannot be called cerebellar while the limb is this weak
question.explanation: Coordination can only be judged in a limb strong enough to perform the task. With power of 3 out of 5 and brisk reflexes, the arm has an upper motor neuron weakness, and that weakness alone can make movements inaccurate, so calling the overshoot cerebellar would send you to the wrong level of the neuraxis. Chorea is a random, flowing extra movement and does not look like overshoot on a target task. Normal clumsiness for age does not come with one-sided weakness and brisk reflexes.

sections.title: The cerebellum's own localizing rules
sections.content:
Students are often surprised by the first of the cerebellum's localizing rules, which is that **cerebellar signs are on the same side as the lesion** (Pearl 2014, p. 63). DeMyer is just as firm, since in his account a unilateral cerebellar lesion causes only ipsilateral cerebellar signs (DeMyer, p. 339).

**Why the same side**

The explanation lies in a double crossing of the pathway. Cerebellar output leaves through the superior cerebellar peduncle and crosses in the midbrain to reach the opposite thalamus and motor cortex. That cortex then sends its corticospinal tract down, crossing again in the medulla, back to the side where the cerebellum began, so the two crossings cancel each other out. A lesion anywhere on that outflow path below the second crossing shows its clumsiness on the side of the cerebellum that started it.

**Midline or hemisphere**

The second rule maps the cerebellum from medial to lateral. The midline vermis and the flocculonodular lobe look after the trunk, stance and eye movements, while the hemispheres plan and tune the limbs (Pearl 2014, p. 63), and the pattern of ataxia follows from that division.

- **Midline lesions** give truncal ataxia, with axial unsteadiness and a wide-based, staggering gait but little ataxia of the limbs when they are tested lying down (Brazis 2011, pp. 411-412), and often nystagmus, vertigo, nausea and vomiting (Pearl 2014, p. 63).
- **Hemispheric lesions** give limb ataxia on the same side, with dysmetria, intention tremor and poor rapid alternating movements (Brazis 2011, p. 412).
- **Both at once**, a pancerebellar syndrome, suggests something diffuse, such as a toxin or drug, a metabolic or inherited disorder, or multiple sclerosis (DeMyer, p. 339).

**A correction worth making**

Some teaching texts, Pearl's among them, say that cerebellar output is entirely inhibitory (Pearl 2014, p. 63). That is true of the cerebellar cortex's own output, from the Purkinje cells to the deep nuclei. The deep nuclei, which carry the cerebellum's message to the rest of the brain, are excitatory in all their projections except those to the inferior olive (Brazis 2011, p. 405). The distinction matters if you want to understand why a cerebellar lesion leaves the motor cortex under-driven rather than released.

**In a child**

The caudal vermis syndrome, in which the child staggers while the limbs are relatively spared, is typical of a medulloblastoma, the classic midline tumor of childhood (Brazis 2011, p. 412). A child who walks badly but performs heel-shin well lying down has already told you that the lesion is in the middle.
keyPoints: Cerebellar signs appear on the same side as the lesion (Pearl 2014, p. 63), because the outflow pathway crosses twice.
Midline lesions give truncal and gait ataxia with relatively spared limbs, and hemispheric lesions give limb ataxia on the same side (Brazis 2011, pp. 411-412).
Bilateral, pancerebellar signs suggest a diffuse cause such as a toxin, a drug, or a metabolic, inherited or demyelinating disorder (DeMyer, p. 339).
The deep nuclei carry the cerebellar output and are excitatory except in their projections to the inferior olive (Brazis 2011, p. 405), and only the Purkinje stage before them is inhibitory.

question.question: A 5-year-old has a month of morning vomiting and now staggers and sways when standing, on a broad base. Lying down, finger-nose and heel-shin are nearly normal on both sides. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
options: The cerebellar vermis in the midline
The dorsal columns of the spinal cord
question.explanation: Ataxia of stance and gait with relatively spared limb coordination is the midline, truncal pattern, and together with morning vomiting it raises the possibility of a midline posterior fossa tumor blocking the fourth ventricle, such as a medulloblastoma (Brazis 2011, p. 412). A right hemispheric lesion would show right limb ataxia on testing. Dorsal column disease causes a sensory ataxia that worsens with the eyes closed and comes with lost position sense, neither of which was described. Disease of both cerebral hemispheres would bring weakness, reflex changes or cognitive signs instead of isolated truncal ataxia.

sections.title: Acute ataxia in a child
sections.content:
A child who could walk yesterday and staggers today is one of the commonest urgent problems in child neurology, and the problem tests whether you can think about level and tempo at the same time. The level is usually the cerebellum or its connections. The tempo, which is acute, narrows the mechanisms to a short list that you can work through in order of danger and of likelihood.

**The short list**

- **An ingestion.** A toddler with sudden ataxia and drowsiness should be assumed to have taken something until there is good reason to think otherwise, because many sedatives and antiseizure drugs cause a pancerebellar picture.
- **Post-infectious cerebellar ataxia.** This is an immune-mediated ataxia that follows a viral illness, and Pearl lists it among the infectious causes of cerebellar disease (Pearl 2014, p. 63). The child is alert, the ataxia is mostly truncal, and the rest of the exam is normal.
- **Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia.** Chaotic, darting, multidirectional eye movements and jerks of the trunk and limbs in an irritable child make up this pattern, and it is a reason to look for a neuroblastoma.
- **A posterior fossa tumor.** The story is usually one of weeks rather than days, often with headache and vomiting from raised intracranial pressure (Brazis 2011, p. 412), and a child who seems to have become ataxic overnight may have been compensating for longer.
- **Something outside the cerebellum.** Absent reflexes with ataxia point to the peripheral nerves, as in a variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome, lost position sense points to a sensory ataxia, and a weak leg can masquerade as ataxia.

**What to do first**

Start with the level of consciousness, and ask specifically what medicines and substances are in the house. Then look at the eyes for nystagmus and opsoclonus, and at the optic discs for papilledema. Check the reflexes, position sense and strength to make sure the ataxia is truly cerebellar. A child who is drowsy or getting worse, or who has papilledema, focal signs or a severe headache, needs urgent imaging, whereas an alert child with isolated truncal ataxia after a viral illness and an otherwise normal exam can often be watched closely.

**Why the order matters**

Acute ataxia rewards the discipline this whole curriculum asks for. The commonest cause is benign, and it is tempting to stop there once it seems to fit. Asking in turn whether the child is safe, whether this is really the cerebellum, and what else keeps it company is what finds the ingestion, the tumor and the neuroblastoma.
keyPoints: In a toddler with acute ataxia, especially with drowsiness, an ingestion should be considered first.
Post-infectious ataxia follows a viral illness in an alert child, with mostly truncal ataxia and an otherwise normal exam (Pearl 2014, p. 63).
Chaotic multidirectional eye movements with myoclonus suggest opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia, which should prompt a search for a neuroblastoma.
Drowsiness, papilledema, focal signs or a worsening course call for urgent imaging.

question.question: A 2-year-old has become unsteady over three days and is irritable. His eyes make rapid, chaotic, conjugate darting movements in all directions, and his trunk and limbs jerk. Reflexes are normal and there was no access to medicines. What should the next step include?
options: Reassurance and review in two weeks for post-infectious ataxia
Nerve conduction studies for a variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome
question.explanation: Chaotic, multidirectional darting eye movements (opsoclonus) with myoclonus and ataxia make up the opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome, which in a young child should prompt a search for a neuroblastoma. Treating it as simple post-infectious ataxia ignores the eye sign that defines the syndrome. A lumbar puncture on its own does nothing to find the tumor that may be driving it. Normal reflexes argue against a Guillain-Barré variant, and opsoclonus is not part of that disorder.

sections.title: Telling central vertigo from peripheral
sections.content:
Vertigo is an illusion of movement, and the first localizing question is whether the illusion starts in the ear and its nerve or in the brainstem and cerebellum that read their signals. Two features of the story answer it, the **time** course of the vertigo and the **company** it keeps.

**Time**

An acute vestibular lesion begins abruptly and then fades as the brain compensates for the lost input (Pearl 2014, p. 119). Peripheral vertigo is therefore worst at the start and eases over days, and Pearl gives vestibular neuronitis four to ten days (Pearl 2014, p. 121). The converse is just as useful, because continuous dizziness that never fluctuates over long periods does not follow the vestibular pattern (Pearl 2014, p. 119) and should make you look elsewhere.

**The eyes**

[[m07-brainstem|Module 7]] listed the nystagmus pearls, and two of them carry most of the weight here. Fixation suppresses peripheral nystagmus but not central nystagmus, and pure vertical or pure torsional nystagmus is central (Brazis 2011, p. 265). Pearl warns that in the very first hours fixation may fail to suppress even a peripheral nystagmus (Pearl 2014, p. 120), so it is worth looking again later.

**Company**

Pearl and Emsellem attach their rule, "the company you keep", to central nystagmus (Pearl 2014, p. 121). Hearing loss and tinnitus keep company with the ear (Pearl 2014, p. 119), while double vision, slurred speech, facial numbness and limb ataxia keep company with the brainstem and cerebellum. The figure weighs the features in the same way, so as you tick what you see, notice that a single central feature overrules any number of peripheral ones.

**The mimic that matters**

A cerebellar infarct can closely mimic acute labyrinthitis, producing vertigo, nausea and vomiting, sometimes with no limb ataxia at all. What betrays it is nystagmus that changes direction, a sign that is found only if someone looks for it (Pearl 2014, pp. 121-122). In children the central cause not to miss is a **posterior fossa tumor**, which is common in childhood (Pearl 2014, p. 63), and Brazis counts posterior fossa tumors, Chiari malformations and cerebellar malformations among the commonest central causes of dizziness in children (Brazis 2011, p. 355).

**Recurrent spells in a child**

Brief, recurrent attacks have a different tempo and a different list. Brazis considers vestibular migraine probably the commonest cause of recurrent vertigo in children (Brazis 2011, p. 354). He also describes **benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood**, in which short spells, sometimes in clusters, leave the child looking frightened, pale and sweaty but fully aware, and which is probably a precursor of migraine (Brazis 2011, p. 355). Between spells the child should be normal, and an abnormal exam means that the company has changed and the address has changed with it.
keyPoints: An acute vestibular lesion eases as the brain compensates, so unremitting dizziness that never fluctuates does not fit the vestibular pattern (Pearl 2014, p. 119).
Fixation suppresses peripheral nystagmus but not central nystagmus, and pure vertical or torsional nystagmus is central (Brazis 2011, p. 265).
A cerebellar infarct can mimic labyrinthitis, and direction-changing nystagmus is the sign that gives it away (Pearl 2014, pp. 121-122).
In children, a posterior fossa tumor is the central cause not to miss (Pearl 2014, p. 63; Brazis 2011, p. 355).
Brief recurrent spells with a normal exam in between suggest vestibular migraine or benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood (Brazis 2011, pp. 354-355).

question.question: A 7-year-old has had three days of vertigo and vomiting after a cold. Hearing is normal and finger-nose is accurate. Her nystagmus beats to the left on left gaze and to the right on right gaze. What should you do?
options: Diagnose vestibular neuritis and expect recovery within days
Perform a positional maneuver for benign positional vertigo
Reassure the family that this is benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood
Treat it as central and image the posterior fossa
question.explanation: Nystagmus that changes direction with gaze is central, and it is exactly the sign that separates a cerebellar lesion from the labyrinthitis it otherwise mimics (Pearl 2014, pp. 121-122). In a child the cause to exclude is a posterior fossa tumor (Pearl 2014, p. 63). Vestibular neuritis is the tempting reading after a cold, and normal limb coordination makes it more tempting still, but its nystagmus beats in one direction only (Pearl 2014, p. 120), and limb ataxia can be absent in a cerebellar infarct as well (Pearl 2014, p. 122). A positional maneuver does not explain constant nystagmus that depends on the direction of gaze. Benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood comes in brief, recurrent spells rather than three continuous days (Brazis 2011, p. 355).

sections.title: The basal ganglia, from too little movement to too much
sections.content:
Where the cerebellum governs how accurately a movement is made, the basal ganglia govern how much movement occurs and which movement is chosen. Their disorders fall along a single axis, and Pearl uses it to sort the whole field into **hypokinetic** disorders, with too little movement, and **hyperkinetic** disorders, with movements that should not be there (Pearl 2014, p. 116).

**Two ends of the axis**

- **Too little** movement shows as slowness, cogwheel rigidity, a tremor at rest, and a stooped, shuffling gait that cannot easily stop (Pearl 2014, p. 116). This is the adult Parkinson picture, and it is rare in childhood.
- **Too much** movement includes chorea (brief, random, flowing movements that dart from one body part to another), dystonia (sustained or repeated twisting postures, often provoked by a particular action), tics, myoclonus and athetosis, and it is this end of the axis that dominates in children.

**Why the involuntary movement is the localizing sign**

There is no weakness to measure and often no change in the reflexes, so the movement itself has to carry the address. Chorea, dystonia and a tremor at rest place the lesion in the subcortex and deep gray matter, the one level where the [[m03-first-fork|localizer]] keeps them. The skill lies in describing the movement precisely before naming it, which means noting what part moves, whether it is brief or sustained, random or patterned, at rest or on action, and whether it can be suppressed.

**Sydenham chorea**

The classic childhood example is Sydenham chorea, a post-streptococcal disorder that Pearl calls pathognomonic of acute rheumatic fever (Pearl 2014, p. 116). A school-aged child becomes fidgety and clumsy, drops things, cannot keep the tongue protruded and grips with a squeeze that waxes and wanes, and behavior and mood often change too. The localization is the basal ganglia, but the diagnosis obliges you to look for the rest of rheumatic fever, including the heart.

**Other childhood patterns**

Dystonia that fluctuates through the day, dyskinetic cerebral palsy after injury to the deep gray matter around birth, and movement disorders that arrive with regression all point to the same level but to very different mechanisms. Placing them at that level begins the reasoning without finishing it, and [[m11-where-to-what|tempo]] is what will divide them.
keyPoints: Basal ganglia disorders sit on one axis, running from hypokinetic disorders with too little movement to hyperkinetic disorders with unwanted movement (Pearl 2014, p. 116).
In children the hyperkinetic end dominates, with chorea, dystonia, tics and myoclonus.
A movement should be described precisely, including which part moves, whether it is brief or sustained, random or patterned, and at rest or on action, before it is named.
Sydenham chorea is post-streptococcal and pathognomonic of acute rheumatic fever, so the rest of the disease must be sought (Pearl 2014, p. 116).

question.question: A 9-year-old girl has three weeks of fidgety, irregular movements flitting between her hands, face and feet, a fluctuating hand grip, and new tearfulness. She had a sore throat six weeks ago. Strength and reflexes are normal. After placing the lesion in the basal ganglia, what is the most important next step?
options: Look for the other features of acute rheumatic fever, including the heart
Reassure the family that this is a tic disorder
question.explanation: Random, flowing movements that pass from one body part to another are chorea, and after a recent sore throat the leading cause is Sydenham chorea, which Pearl calls pathognomonic of acute rheumatic fever (Pearl 2014, p. 116). Making that diagnosis obliges you to look for carditis and the rest of the disease. The spinal cord cannot generate chorea. Tics are patterned, repetitive and briefly suppressible, unlike these flitting movements, and calling this a tic disorder would miss the heart. Nerve conduction studies examine the motor unit, which is not the level involved here.

sections.title: Gait as the integrator
sections.content:
If you could watch a child do only one thing, walking would be the one to choose. Gait is an excellent screen of the whole motor system (Pearl 2014, p. 114), and because lesions at each level of the neuraxis impair it in a characteristic way, the features of a gait suggest both the location of the lesion and its probable cause (DeMyer, p. 338). Pearl teaches gait from the bottom up, from muscle to cortex (Pearl 2014, pp. 114-117), which turns it into a tour of the eleven levels.

**Bottom up**

- **Muscle** weakness gives a waddling, sway-backed gait from weak hip muscles, and the classic boy with Duchenne dystrophy has big calves, lordosis and a waddle (Pearl 2014, p. 115).
- **Junction** disease gives a gait that fatigues and recovers with rest.
- **Nerve** disease gives a steppage gait, with the knee lifted high to clear a dropped foot.
- **Root** disease gives an antalgic gait that avoids weight on a painful leg.
- **Cord** disease gives a stiff, scissoring gait from spasticity.
- **Basal ganglia** disease gives a dancing, choreic gait, or a shuffling one.
- **Cerebellar** disease gives a wide-based gait that cannot manage heel to toe.
- **Hemisphere** lesions give a circumducting gait, with the stiff leg swung outward.

The figure above lets you pick a gait and see the level it points to and the company it keeps.

**The developing gait**

A child's gait also follows a developmental timetable of its own. The newborn steps reflexly when held upright, cruising follows, and around the first birthday the toddler walks freely on a broad base with short, jerky steps and frequent falls, developing the mature heel-toe stride with swinging arms only later (DeMyer, p. 338). A broad-based, falling gait is therefore normal at thirteen months and an abnormal sign at five years.

**Toe walking**

Toe walking is the best example of a gait that does not localize on its own. It can be the first sign of Duchenne dystrophy or of spastic diplegia, it is common in autism, and in a child who runs, skips and hops normally it may be an idiosyncratic, sometimes familial pattern with no disease at all (DeMyer, p. 338). Which of these it is depends on the rest of the examination.

**How to look**

Ask the child to walk, to run, to walk on the heels and on the toes, and to walk heel to toe. Heel and toe walking test the muscles of the sciatic territory as well as balance (DeMyer, p. 338), and the examination goes better with young children if you turn it into a race or a game.
keyPoints: Gait screens the whole motor system, and its features suggest both the level and the cause of a lesion (DeMyer, p. 338; Pearl 2014, p. 114).

From the bottom up, the gaits are the waddle of muscle, the fatigable gait of the junction, the steppage of nerve, the antalgic gait of root, the scissoring of cord, the choreic gait of the basal ganglia, the wide-based gait of the cerebellum and the circumducting gait of the hemisphere.
A broad-based, falling toddler gait is normal around the first birthday (DeMyer, p. 338).
Toe walking does not localize on its own and may reflect Duchenne dystrophy, spastic diplegia, autism or an idiopathic familial pattern (DeMyer, p. 338).

question.question: A 4-year-old is referred for toe walking. He runs, skips, hops on either foot and can stand flat-footed. He rises from the floor without using his hands, his calves are normal in size, and reflexes and plantars are normal. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Spastic diplegia from periventricular white-matter injury
An idiosyncratic or familial toe-walking pattern without neurological disease
question.explanation: Toe walking needs the rest of the exam before it localizes. A child who runs, skips and hops normally, rises without a Gowers maneuver and has normal tone and reflexes shows none of the serious causes, and DeMyer describes exactly this child as having an idiosyncratic, sometimes familial gait (DeMyer, p. 338). Duchenne dystrophy would usually show proximal weakness and enlarged calves. Spastic diplegia would bring increased tone and brisk reflexes in the legs. A neuropathy tends to cause foot drop and a steppage gait, which is the opposite of toe walking.

quiz.question: A 12-year-old has a coarse tremor of the right hand that is absent at rest and grows larger as her finger approaches your finger. Which level does this tremor point to?
options: The right cerebellar hemisphere or its outflow
quiz.explanation: A tremor that appears on action and worsens near the target is an intention tremor, which is a cerebellar sign. Cerebellar signs lie on the same side as the lesion, so a tremor of the right hand points to the right cerebellar hemisphere or its outflow. A basal ganglia tremor is typically present at rest. A left cerebellar lesion would affect the left limbs. A median nerve lesion causes weakness and numbness, and it does not produce an intention tremor.

quiz.question: A 15-year-old started a new antiseizure medicine a week ago and is now unsteady, with slurred speech, nystagmus in every direction of gaze, and ataxia of all four limbs. Which reading fits best?
options: A pancerebellar syndrome from a drug effect
A lesion of the left medial longitudinal fasciculus
quiz.explanation: Bilateral, symmetric cerebellar signs make up a pancerebellar syndrome, which suggests a diffuse cause such as a toxin or drug rather than a focal lesion (DeMyer, p. 339), and some antiseizure drugs also cause a central-type nystagmus (Pearl 2014, p. 121). A hemispheric tumor would give limb signs on the same side as the tumor. A midline lesion would spare the limbs more than this. A lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus causes an internuclear ophthalmoplegia, which would not explain ataxia in all four limbs.

quiz.question: A 13-year-old stands steadily with her eyes open but sways and nearly falls when she closes them. Vibration and position sense are lost in the toes, and the ankle reflexes are absent. Finger-nose is accurate. What kind of ataxia is this?
options: Sensory ataxia from the large sensory nerves or dorsal columns
quiz.explanation: Steadiness with the eyes open that fails with the eyes closed is a positive Romberg sign, meaning that vision was compensating for lost position sense. With absent vibration and position sense and lost ankle reflexes, this is a sensory ataxia arising from the large sensory nerves or the dorsal columns. A patient with cerebellar ataxia is unsteady with the eyes open as well and more or less passes a Romberg test (DeMyer, p. 339). Nothing in the examination is inconsistent or effortful in a way that would suggest a functional disorder.

quiz.question: A 10-year-old with high-arched feet lifts both knees high and slaps the feet down when walking. Ankle reflexes are absent and the calves are thin. Which level does the gait point to?
quiz.explanation: Lifting the knees high to clear dropped feet is a steppage gait, the gait of the peripheral nerve (Pearl 2014, p. 115). Bilateral foot drop with high arches, thin calves and absent ankle reflexes suggests a symmetric, length-dependent neuropathy, which is often inherited, as in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (DeMyer, p. 338). A cerebellar gait is wide-based rather than high-stepping. A cord lesion causes a stiff, scissoring gait with brisk reflexes. Muscle disease usually gives a proximal waddle.

quiz.question: Which statement about cerebellar output is accurate?
options: All cerebellar output is inhibitory, so a cerebellar lesion releases the motor cortex
Cerebellar output reaches the opposite cortex without crossing
Purkinje cells inhibit the deep nuclei, and the deep nuclei excite their targets, except the inferior olive
The deep nuclei are inhibitory and the Purkinje cells excitatory
quiz.explanation: The cerebellar cortex speaks only through the Purkinje cells, which inhibit the deep cerebellar nuclei. The deep nuclei then carry the cerebellum's output, and all of their projections are excitatory except those to the inferior olive (Brazis 2011, p. 405). The claim that all output is inhibitory, found in some primers, confuses the Purkinje stage with the final output. The outflow does cross, in the midbrain, and that crossing is half of the double crossing that keeps cerebellar signs on the same side. The statement that the deep nuclei are inhibitory and the Purkinje cells excitatory simply reverses the two stages.

quiz.question: A 13-month-old who started walking three weeks ago walks on a broad base with short, jerky, irregular steps, arms held up and slightly flexed, and falls every few steps. Strength, tone and reflexes are normal. What do you conclude?
options: Midline cerebellar ataxia, calling for imaging of the posterior fossa
A normal toddler gait for age
quiz.explanation: A broad base, short jerky steps, raised arms and frequent falls make up the normal toddler gait when independent walking begins, around the first birthday (DeMyer, p. 338). The same gait at five would be an abnormal sign, but at thirteen months, with a normal exam, it is ordinary development. Calling it cerebellar ataxia ignores the child's age. Spastic diplegia would bring stiff legs and brisk reflexes. A myopathy would show weakness and difficulty rising from the floor.

quiz.question: A 3-year-old has brief spells every few weeks: she suddenly looks frightened, clings to her mother, turns pale and sweaty, and cannot stand steadily, then is herself again within minutes. She stays responsive throughout. Her examination between spells is normal. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Focal seizures arising from the temporal lobe
quiz.explanation: Brief recurrent spells of vertigo in which a young child looks frightened, pale and sweaty without losing awareness, with a normal exam between them, match the picture Brazis gives for benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood, which is probably a migraine precursor (Brazis 2011, p. 355). A posterior fossa tumor is the dangerous alternative to keep in mind, but brief spells with full recovery and a normal examination between them do not fit a growing mass, and a sign that persisted between spells would change the answer. Vestibular neuritis is a single episode that eases over days (Pearl 2014, p. 121). Temporal lobe seizures can cause vertigo, but Brazis advises looking for staring, automatisms or other temporal lobe features, and none are present here (Brazis 2011, p. 355).

signOff: The resident describes the gait of five children in level terms before any other part of the exam, and a faculty member agrees.

opener.parable: The cerebellum and the basal ganglia don't move a limb by themselves. They shape movements that begin elsewhere, adjusting their timing, force and smoothness, which is why damage to them can leave a child able to move but unable to move well.
opener.history: Gordon Holmes (1876–1965), whose scheme of examination underlies the one neurologists still use, described how a cerebellar patient breaks a movement into pieces, reaching the nose in two separate steps instead of one smooth curve.
